Definition

  • Infections that require surgical therapy.
  • Infections that affect surgical patients.
  • Surgical infection = any infection affecting a surgical patient, whether present before, during, or after surgery: pre-existing infection/abscess at the operative site, SSI, hospital-acquired pneumonia/VAP, UTI/CAUTI, C. difficile infection, CLABSI, other hospital/ICU infections.
  • UTI acquired during admission for investigation of a liver mass = nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infection. 432 ×4

Infection control & prevention

  • Hand hygiene — the most effective measure.
  • Universal precautions.
  • Contact isolation: MRSA, VRE, MDR-GNB.
  • Avoid catheters; proper insertion and dressing; early removal.
  • Replace lines that were inserted without proper preparation.
  • Careful dressing maintenance.
  • Ventilator weaning; 1 day of intubation = 1–3% risk of pneumonia.
  • Selective use of antibiotic therapy.
  • Remember: wash your hands.
  • ⭐ Exam: the most effective infection-prevention measure = hand hygiene — repeatedly asked.
  • Infection control aims to prevent infection rather than treat it. Every catheter/line/drain increases infection risk.
  • Most effective measure to prevent surgical infection after an uncomplicated lap appendectomy → hand hygiene. 437
  • Diabetic with pain/erythema at a lipoma-excision site, otherwise well → source key proper hand hygiene. 439
  • Universal precautions: never re-sheath needles. 438
  • Blood transfusion can transmit hepatitis B (also C, HIV). 426

Risk factors for surgical infection

  • Extremes of age (neonates, > 65 years).
  • Malnutrition. Obesity. Diabetes mellitus.
  • Prior site irradiation.
  • Hypothermia. Hypoxemia.
  • Coexisting infection remote to the surgical site.
  • Corticosteroid therapy.
  • Recent operation, especially of chest or abdomen.
  • Chronic inflammation.
  • Hypocholesterolemia.
  • Among diabetes, hypertension, high bilirubin and anemia, diabetes significantly increases wound-infection risk. 430
  • Tight glucose control decreases deep wound infection. 438

Diagnosis

  • Surgical infections are primarily clinical diagnoses (history and examination); investigations confirm/localize and guide management.
  • Core principle: treat the patient, not an isolated lab/imaging finding. A positive culture or imaging abnormality alone does not necessarily mean established infection.
  • A single blood culture growing S. epidermidis in a patient with no signs of infection = likely contaminant → proceed with discharge. 437 ×2

Classification of surgical wounds

Classification of surgical wounds (slide 8)

ClassDefinition (doctor)SSI risk / prophylaxis
1. CleanNo hollow viscus entered; no inflammation/infection; no break in aseptic technique; usually elective, primary closure (mastectomy, thyroidectomy)~1–3%; prophylaxis usually not needed unless prosthetic/foreign material
2. Clean-contaminatedControlled entry into a hollow viscus/colonized tract without significant contamination (controlled bowel resection, cholecystectomy)Prophylaxis generally indicated
3. ContaminatedUncontrolled/gross spillage from a viscus; fresh open traumatic wound; major break in sterile technique; acute non-purulent inflammationHigher SSI risk
4. Dirty/infectedEstablished infection, pus/abscess, perforated viscus, old heavily contaminated traumatic wound~30–40%; treatment, not prophylaxis
  • General principle: the deeper/more contaminated the operation, the higher the infection risk.
  • Clean-contaminated: controlled colectomy (with irrigation), elective sigmoidectomy, lap cholecystectomy (even emergency, for acute cholecystitis without spillage/pus). 442 441 442 426
  • Clean: elective thyroidectomy. 441
  • Fecal spillage in the OR → contaminated (class 3). 441
  • High-risk procedure for infection: traumatic tracheoesophageal fistula (contaminated/dirty). 437

Principles of antibiotic therapy

Prophylaxis

  • Reduces SSI. Does NOT reduce nosocomial infections.
  • Indicated for most clean-contaminated or contaminated procedures, and for clean procedures with prosthetic grafts.
  • First-generation cephalosporin is preferred. Clindamycin for penicillin-allergic patients.
  • Second-generation cephalosporins are used to cover GN or anaerobes (or first-gen + metronidazole).
  • Give within 1 hour of incision; re-dose every 3–4 hours intra-operatively.
ScenarioAgent (doctor)
Common prophylaxisCefazolin (1st-generation cephalosporin)
Significant β-lactam allergyClindamycin, depending on procedure/protocol
Bowel proceduresBowel-flora cover including anaerobes (metronidazole) ± cephalosporin
  • Penicillin allergy + AAA repair with synthetic graft → clindamycin. 437
  • Uncomplicated lap appendectomy → peri-op ceftriaxone + metronidazole, no 72-hour course. 439
  • Appendectomy regimen → cephalosporin + metronidazole (gram-negatives + anaerobes/bacteroides). 429
  • Stab wound with bowel evisceration → ceftriaxone + metronidazole. 437
  • The commonest organism in the large bowel = Bacteroides. 430 ×2
  • A therapeutic antibiotic course is indicated for open appendectomy for perforated appendicitis (dirty) — not for clean/clean-contaminated cases. 431 ×3

Treatment

  • Careful clinical evaluation. Empirical therapy with high suspicion. Cultures BEFORE starting antibiotics. Clinical- and culture-guided therapy.
Agent/pathogen factorsPatient factors
Activity against known/suspected pathogensSeverity of illness
Disease believed responsibleAge
Infection vs colonizationImmunosuppression
Narrow-spectrum coverage bestOrgan dysfunction
Antimicrobial resistance patternsAllergy
  • Established infection ≠ prophylaxis — needs therapeutic antibiotics. Severe sepsis: cultures when feasible, start broad empiric therapy promptly, then narrow to culture-directed therapy.
  • Hospital-acquired infections may need broader initial cover than community-acquired.
  • Rising creatinine on amoxicillin + metronidazole + gentamicin → stop gentamicin (nephrotoxic). 431 ×2
  • Anaphylaxis (SOB, hypotension) on starting IV penicillin → stop penicillin immediately first. 435 ×6
  • Sudden SOB, wheeze, cyanosis and hypotension after starting antibiotics → anaphylactic shock. 430
  • Variceal bleed: the IV drug shown to reduce mortality → ceftriaxone (antibiotic prophylaxis). 438 ×3

Surgical site infection (SSI)

  • A clinical diagnosis.
  • Most common cause of delay in wound healing.
  • Superficial — skin and subcutaneous tissue. Deep — fascia and muscle. Organ space — internal organs (cavities).
  • Rare in the first few days after surgery EXCEPT necrotizing soft-tissue infection (necrotizing fasciitis) — caused by S. pyogenes or C. perfringens — can appear in the first 24 hours.
  • Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency; delay increases mortality.
  • Presenting features depend on depth: pain-related immobility, wound drainage, crepitus, blisters/bullae; SIRS/sepsis; organ-specific symptoms.
  • Management: local wound care, antibiotics, imaging, formal debridement, drainage, healing by secondary intention.
DepthTypical findings (doctor)Management
SuperficialLocal erythema, minor wound separation, local discharge; patient eating/functioning normallyLocal wound care
DeeperMore tenderness, deep pain, guarding, pusOpen/drain, investigate
Organ-spaceSystemically unwell despite a normal-looking wound — rigors, fever, ileus, vomitingImaging + source control (drainage)
  • Wounds expected to heal in ~3–6 weeks but failing to progress → suspect infection.
  • Avoid routine dressing disturbance in the first ~72 hours (acute inflammatory phase) unless indicated — ordinary SSIs don't present that early.
  • ⭐ Severe infection within ~24 h → think necrotizing fasciitis. Escalate to seniors and go to the OR urgently — don't wait for unnecessary investigations.
  • Principle: the deeper the infection, the more invasive the approach.
  • A radiology request should ask a specific clinical question; review the images yourself.
  • Post-op superficial SSI with pus, erythema and fever (day 3–5) → open the wound (remove sutures) and drain; don't just change/increase antibiotics. 441 434 ×4 431 ×2 430
  • Purulent discharge, patient stable and afebrile (POD 5) → open and clean the wound at the bedside, regular dressings. 442
  • Erythema/pain without pus or fever (lipoma, laparotomy) → superficial skin infection → local wound care / daily cleansing. 437 439 437 ×2
  • Crepitus, bullae, dusky skin, severe pain after a lipoma excision or hernia repair → necrotizing fasciitis → broad-spectrum antibiotics + urgent surgical debridement. 442 442 ×2
  • Rapidly progressive leg swelling over 2 days with severe pain and black blisters → necrotizing fasciitis. 438 Final
  • Infected sutured wound (diabetic, sutured late) that is opened and dressed → healing shows a prolonged proliferation phase (healing by secondary intention). 432 Final ×2
  • Diabetic heel wound with crepitus, discoloration, fever → Clostridium perfringens (gas gangrene). 431 ×3
  • Progressive redness, pain and fever after a knife prick → cellulitis 431 ×3; treat with penicillin G. 430 ×2
  • Swelling on the nape/back with multiple discharging openings (diabetic) → carbuncle. 438 ×4 430 ×2
  • Tetanus from a foot wound: first step airway and ventilation. 430 ×2
  • Dirty wound (mud, soil, oil, grass) with unknown tetanus vaccination → give tetanus toxoid + tetanus immunoglobulin. 436 Final

Intra-abdominal infection

  • Usually following abdominal surgery. Abscess vs general peritonitis. Variable clinical manifestations.
  • Treatment: broad-spectrum antibiotics + drainage, surgical intervention, or both. Delay causes higher morbidity and mortality.
  • Frequently needs source control, not antibiotics alone — percutaneous drain, operative drainage, or surgery.
  • Fever + RLQ pain after lap appendectomy for perforation, wound fine → intra-abdominal abscess. 439
  • 6-cm RLQ collection, stable → antibiotics + percutaneous drainage. 441
  • Large 12×18 cm collection 3 weeks after laparotomy → percutaneous drainage (compilers: not sure). 434
  • Appendicitis with pus collection and shock → definitive step = drainage of the abscess (source control). 431 ×3
  • Fever, tachycardia and hiccups 10 days after sleeve gastrectomy → CT abdomen for leak/abscess. 437

Urinary tract infection

  • Rare in non-catheterized ICU patients.
  • Bacteriuria/candiduria ± pyuria ≠ established surgical infection.
  • In ICU, MDR organisms more commonly cause UTI in catheterized patients.
  • Prevention: avoid catheters if possible; short duration (< 48 h); careful catheter care (sterile gloves).
  • UTI in men is uncommon without a catheter; women develop UTI more commonly. Positive urine findings alone don't equal significant infection.
  • CAUTI: avoid unnecessary catheterization; remove as soon as the indication ends.
  • Most common cause of catheter-associated UTI (keyed) → improper catheterization technique. 436 Final

Post-operative pneumonia — VAP

  • Ventilator-associated pneumonia occurs 2–3 days after intubation.
  • Most common surgical infection in ICU.
  • Late VAP (> 5 days) — likely MDR bacteria.
  • Prevention: avoid if possible; shorter intubation; orotracheal better than nasotracheal; standard weaning protocols.
  • Longer intubation → greater risk. Extubate as early as safely possible, even on the operating table.
  • Most common ICU infection in a ventilated burn patient → VAP. 442
  • Preventing VAP → daily sedation interruption / daily trial of extubation, head elevated 30–45° (not below). 439

Post-operative fever

  • Fever 48 hours (POD 2) after surgery → atelectasis is the classic answer. 441 ×12 442

Central line–associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI)

  • S. epidermidis and other gram-positive cocci — most common.
  • A single positive culture could be a contaminant.
  • GNB: less common, but almost never contaminants.
  • Fungal CLABSI: in critically ill patients at risk.
  • Treatment: catheter removal; antibiotic course — usually long.
  • Prevention: proper insertion technique.
  • Coagulase-negative staph may be true infection or contamination — interpret a single positive culture in context.
  • TPN through a PICC, fever, 2 blood cultures with S. aureus → remove the PICC, send the tip for culture, give antibiotics. 439 ×9
  • PICC infection not responding to antibiotics → remove the PICC. 435 Final; redness, swelling and pus at a peripheral IV site → remove the IV line and start antibiotics. 436 Final
  • Persistent hyperglycemia on TPN despite insulin → look for a source of sepsis. 438 ×4

C. difficile

  • Diarrhea with mucus after an IV cephalosporin course → Clostridium difficile (pseudomembranous colitis). 439 ×8
  • Bloody diarrhea, mucus, fever, tachycardia and C. difficile cytotoxin in the stool → pseudomembranous colitis. 429 Final
  • Mild–moderate CDI → oral vancomycin or oral fidaxomicin (and stop the offending antibiotic if possible). 442

SIRS, sepsis & septic shock (from past exams)

  • SIRS = ≥2 of: temperature >38 or <36, HR >90, RR >20 (or PaCO₂ <32), WBC >12,000 or <4,000. Post-op HR 110, RR 25, T 38.5, WBC 13,000 with normal BP → SIRS. 442 432 ×3 441
  • Fever, tachycardia and organ dysfunction (rising urea/creatinine) with MAP 75 → severe sepsis (old terminology). 432 ×2
  • Fever, confusion, BP 80/50 (MAP 55), lactate 4.5 → septic shock. 441 430
  • Septic shock pathophysiology: systemic vasodilation (↓ SVR), hyperdynamic heart, collapsed IVC; peripheral vasodilation; microcirculatory dysfunction (toxic cholangitis). 442 432 ×3 431 ×2
  • Gram-negative bacteremia after splenic rupture + 8 units of blood → bacterial translocation from the bowel. 432 ×2
  • In the SIRS-after-surgery question, the keyed supporting finding was gastroduodenal (stress) ulcer. 441
  • Overwhelming sepsis a year after splenectomy → Streptococcus pneumoniae (encapsulated). 438 ×2
  • Before splenectomy, the best way to reduce future infection → vaccinate against S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis and H. influenzae type b. 442 Final ×2

Other surgical infection pathogens

Susceptible patientsPathogens
Prolonged hospitalizationVRE (vancomycin-resistant enterococci)
Critically illMRSA
Prolonged ICU stay/intubationPseudomonas aeruginosa
Multi-organ involvementMDR Enterobacteriaceae (e.g. Klebsiella)
Multiple courses of antibioticsAcinetobacter baumannii; fungal infection
  • Fungal infection and MDR organisms are more likely with prolonged ICU stay and repeated broad-spectrum antibiotics.

ERAS (doctor)

  • Enhanced Recovery After Surgery began in colorectal surgery: early removal of unnecessary tubes/lines/catheters, early extubation, early mobilization, reducing what delays recovery (including infection).

Summary

  • Surgical infections remain a major cause of morbidity and mortality.
  • The deeper you get, the higher the chance of infection.
  • Any proven infection needs pathogen-directed therapy.
  • Avoid or limit lines, tubes and catheters; remove them if infected.
  • Prevention is the best management strategy. Wash your hands!

Inflammation and Infection in Surgery

Introduction:
  • Three Key Elements in Infection Development

1. Susceptible Host – Individual patient factors influence infection risk.

2. Infectious Agent – The virulence of bacteria affects infection potential.

3. Suitable Medium/Environment – Blood perfusion, oxygenation, and tissue

  • conditions impact bacterial growth.
    • Determinants of Infection Development
    • Bacterial Virulence – Highly pathogenic organisms increase infection risk.
    • Host Immune Response – Effectiveness of chemotaxis, phagocytosis, and B-/T-lymphocyte activation.
    • Local Tissue Conditions – Blood flow & oxygenation levels in the infected area.
  • The susceptible host
  • Many surgical infections occur in patients without immune deficiencies.
  • However, immunocompromised patients (e.g., transplant recipients, HIV, diabetics) are at higher risk of surgical site infections (SSIs).
  • Poorly controlled diabetes exacerbates immune dysfunction more than well-managed diabetes.
  • Perioperative Glucose Control & CDC Guidelines
  • Maintaining glucose levels <200 mg/dL perioperatively reduces SSI risk in both diabetic and non-diabetic patients.
  • The infectious agent
  • Most common organisms
    • Clostridium difficile (12%) – Common in antibiotic-associated infections.
    • Staphylococcus aureus (11%) – Most common cause of surgical site infections (SSIs), with growing antibiotic resistance.
    • Klebsiella pneumoniae (10%) – Frequent in hospital-acquired pneumonia & UTIs.
    • Escherichia coli (9%) – Common in UTIs & intra-abdominal infections.
    • Enterococcus species (9%) – Can cause bloodstream infections & endocarditis.
    • Pseudomonas aeruginosa (7%) – Associated with ventilator- associated pneumonia & wound infections.
    • Candida species (6%) – Fungal infections, especially in immunocompromised patients.
  • Infection types
    • Surgical Site Infections (SSIs)
    • Most common cause: Staphylococcus aureus.
    • Staphylococcus epidermidis (normally nonpathogenic) can cause serious infections in immunosuppressed patients & those with indwelling catheters/implants.
    • Necrotizing Skin & Soft-Tissue Infections
    • Polymicrobial (Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and anaerobes).
    • Monobacterial infections include:
    • Clostridial species (e.g., Clostridium perfringens) – Causes gas gangrene.
    • Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Strep) – Spreads through connective tissue & lymphatics.
    • Intra-Abdominal Infections (Post-GI Surgery)
    • Gram-negative & anaerobic bacteria predominate, including:
    • Bacteroides species.
    • Klebsiella pneumoniae.
    • Enterobacter species.
    • Opportunistic Infections in Immunocompromised & Critically Ill
    • Fungal Infections: Candida, Aspergillus, Histoplasma.
    • Parasitic Infections: Amoeba, Echinococcus (liver abscesses).
  • The suitable medium
  • Conditions Favoring Bacterial Growth
    • Closed space with poor vascular perfusion.
    • Low oxygen tension (hypoxia).
    • Acidic environment (low pH).
    • Ischemic or necrotic tissues provide an optimal bacterial medium.
Surgical site infection (SSI):
  • Types:
  • Criteria:
  • Classification of Wounds:
  • Pathophysiology:
  • Multifactorial Causes of SSIs
    • Patient factors (comorbidities, immune status, endogenous flora).
    • Surgical factors (procedure type, technique, presence of implants).
    • Perioperative environment (hospital infrastructure, OR processes).
  • Risk factors
    • Patient-related:
    • Advanced age.
    • Diabetes mellitus.
    • Obesity.
    • Smoking.
    • Alcoholism.
    • Malnutrition.
    • Immunosuppression:
    • Chronic steroid use.
    • HIV/AIDS.
    • Post-transplant immunosuppressive therapy.
    • Procedure-related:
    • NHSN Risk Index for SSI Prediction
    • Developed to stratify a patient’s risk of developing an SSI preoperatively.
    • Three Major Risk Factors:
    • ASA score ≥3.
    • Surgical wound classification as either contaminated or dirty.
    • Prolonged procedure duration (beyond a set threshold "T" for each procedure type).
    • System-related:
    • Suboptimal choice and timing of antibiotics
    • Proper antibiotic selection.
    • Administration within 60 minutes before incision (or 120 minutes for vancomycin & fluoroquinolones).
    • Appropriate discontinuation of antibiotics postoperatively (to avoid resistance & adverse effects).
    • Unrecognized breach of asepsis
    • Peri-operative hair removal
    • Hair clipping is superior to shaving
    • Surgical technique
    • Operating room design and traffic
    • Includes OR air flow and number of people
  • Prevention
    • Peri-operative antibiotics
    • Infusion must be completed within 1 hour before incision.
    • Vancomycin & fluoroquinolones require administration 2 hours before incision due to longer infusion times.
    • No additional doses are needed after skin closure, even if drains are present.
    • Weight-based dosing & manufacturer guidelines should be followed.
    • Antiseptic skin preparation
    • Adhesive tapes
    • Maintaining normoglycemia
    • Goal: < 200 mg/dl
    • Peri-operative O2 supplementation
    • Administer 80% oxygen intraoperatively and 2–6 hours postoperatively to reduce the risk of surgical site infections (SSIs).
    • Maintaining normothermia
  • Treatment
    • Primary Treatment
    • Open the incision to allow drainage.
    • Drain purulent material & perform debridement of necrotic tissue.
    • Organ-Space SSIs
    • Preferred treatment: Percutaneous drainage under radiologic guidance + appropriate antibiotics.
Infections requiring surgical management
  • Inflammation, sepsis, and septic shock
  • Local Inflammatory Response to Infection
    • Microbial infection causes tissue damage, triggering an immune response to eliminate pathogens.
    • Endothelial cells & leukocytes release inflammatory mediators, including:
    • Cytokines: TNF-α, interleukins, interferons.
    • Lipid-derived mediators: Leukotrienes, prostaglandins.
    • Reactive molecules: Nitric oxide (NO), reactive oxygen species (ROS).
    • Classic inflammatory mediators: Complement proteins, histamine, bradykinin.
    • Function: These mediators recruit immune cells, promote tissue healing, and fight infection.
  • IMP!!!
  • Systemic Inflammatory Response & Sepsis
ConditionDefinition
Systemic Inflammatory ResponseSystemic inflammation without infection (e.g., burns,
Syndrome (SIRS)trauma, pancreatitis).
SepsisSIRS caused by a documented infection.
Septic ShockSepsis with hypotension & hemodynamic instability,
leading to organ failure.
BacteremiaPresence of viable bacteria in the bloodstream, detected by blood cultures.
  • Septic Shock & Organ Dysfunction
    • Can cause multiple organ failure, affecting:
    • Brain → Delirium.
    • Lungs → Hypoxia, respiratory failure.
    • Heart → Hypotension, pulmonary edema.
    • Kidneys → Oliguria, renal failure.
  • Diagnosis
    • Clinical Examination
    • Thorough physical examination.
    • Key findings may include:
    • Localized pain, redness, swelling, or drainage (wound infections, abscesses).
    • Respiratory symptoms (pneumonia, pleural effusions).
    • Neurologic changes (meningitis, encephalitis).
    • Labs
    • Leukocytosis (high WBC count) is common.
    • Leukopenia (low WBC count) may indicate severe infection or sepsis.
    • Acidosis (low pH) may be present & aid in diagnosis.
    • Imaging
Suspected InfectionPreferred Imaging Modality
PneumoniaChest X-ray or CT scan.
Intra-abdominal/Intra-thoracic abscessCT scan or ultrasound.
Osteomyelitis (bone infection)MRI or bone scan.
    • Microbiology
    • Cultures are obtained from the expected source
    • Treatment
    • Antibiotics
Surgical skin and skin structure infections
  • Furuncle
  • Furuncles are superficial skin abscesses caused by Staphylococcus aureus at the hair follicle level.
  • Triggering event: Obstruction of the pilosebaceous unit, leading to localized infection & inflammation.
  • Risk Factors
    • Puberty (hormonal changes affecting sebaceous glands).
    • Male gender.
    • Obesity.
    • Diabetes (impaired immune response).
    • Poor hygiene.
    • Living in humid climates.
  • Most common: Staphylococcus aureus.
  • Others:
    • Streptococci.
    • Gram-negative bacteria.
    • Anaerobic diphtheroids.
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Itchy, indurated small abscess with surrounding erythema.
    • Often presents with a small white necrotic area at the top.
  • Treatment & Management
    • Most furuncles resolve spontaneously.
    • Larger lesions require incision & drainage (I&D).
    • Antibiotics are not routinely needed but may be considered if:
    • Extensive surrounding cellulitis is present.
    • Patient is immunocompromised or has recurrent infections.
  • Carbuncle
  • Carbuncles are a severe form of skin infection resulting from multiple furuncles merging.
  • Risk Factors
    • Most seen on the back of the neck in diabetic or immunocompromised patients.
    • Other risk factors include:
    • Obesity.
    • Diabetes mellitus.
    • Chronic steroid use.
    • Malnutrition.
  • Most common pathogen: Staphylococcus aureus
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Multiple large abscesses with several openings draining pus.
    • Central necrotic tissue due to disrupted blood supply (skin turns white before necrosis).
    • May present with systemic symptoms (fever, malaise).
  • Treatment & Management
    • Incision & drainage (I&D) is required, with extensive excision if deep sinus tracts are involved.
    • Antibiotic therapy is usually needed
  • Hidradenitis Suppurativa
  • A chronic skin condition caused by blockage & infection of apocrine sweat glands.
  • Commonly affects axillae & groin, but also occurs in perineum, inframammary folds, gluteal folds, areola, & scrotum.
  • Risk Factors
    • Obesity.
    • Puberty (hormonal influence).
    • Female gender.
    • Smoking.
  • Causative Organisms
    • Polymicrobial infection involving:
    • Gram-positive bacteria.
    • Gram-negative bacteria.
    • Anaerobes.
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Early stage: Painful, erythematous nodules in areas with apocrine glands.
    • Progression: Deep, indurated abscesses with interconnected sinus tracts & purulent drainage.
    • May be associated with regional lymphadenopathy.
    • Severe scarring may develop over time.
  • Treatment & Management
    • Incision & drainage of abscesses & sinus tracts are required.
    • Chronic & recurrent cases may need:
    • Excision of affected skin & apocrine glands.
    • Healing by secondary intention or skin grafts/flaps for severe scarring.
    • Adjunctive therapies:
    • Topical clindamycin.
    • Systemic tetracyclines.
    • Isotretinoin (for severe cases).
  • Necrotizing skin and soft tissue infections (NSTIs)
  • NSTIs are life-threatening infections characterized by widespread tissue necrosis due to aggressive, toxin-producing bacteria.
  • Also known as:
    • Necrotizing fasciitis (if involving fascial layers).
    • Fournier gangrene (if affecting perineum/genitalia).
    • Ludwig angina (if involving the floor of the mouth).
    • Gas gangrene (if caused by Clostridium species).
  • Common entry points:
    • Puncture wounds, insect bites, perirectal/perianal abscesses.
    • Diabetes and urogenital procedures increase the risk for perineal infections.
    • Rapid progression along ischemic tissue planes, often with gas formation in deeper tissues.
  • Causative Agents
    • Type I NSTI: Monomicrobial (e.g., Streptococcus spp., Clostridium spp.).
    • Type II NSTI: Polymicrobial (gram-positive, gram-negative, anaerobic bacteria).
    • Type III NSTI: Rare; caused by Vibrio vulnificus (from saltwater exposure).
  • Risk Factors
    • Immunocompromised patients (HIV, cancer, diabetes).
    • IV drug use.
    • Malnourished & obese patients.
    • Recent surgery or trauma.
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Early signs:
    • Fever and pain out of proportion to physical findings.
    • Erythema, induration, hemorrhagic bullae, blisters.
    • Grayish skin discoloration suggests deep necrosis.
    • Rapid systemic deterioration:
    • Hypotension, tachycardia, electrolyte imbalances, multi-organ failure.
  • Laboratory Findings:
    • Leukocytosis or leukopenia, hyponatremia, metabolic acidosis.
  • Imaging:
    • CT scan: Gold standard for deep inflammation & gas pockets.
    • "Finger test": Tissue easily separates with minimal resistance.
  • Treatment
    • NSTI is a surgical emergency requiring immediate debridement & antibiotics.
    • Wide Surgical Debridement
    • All necrotic & ischemic tissue must be removed (including overlying skin).
    • Amputation may be needed for extensive limb involvement.
    • Broad-Spectrum Antibiotics
    • Empiric regimen covers gram-positive, gram-negative, & anaerobes:
    • Penicillin-based or cephalosporin + aminoglycoside or fluoroquinolone + metronidazole/clindamycin.
    • Clindamycin: Reduces bacterial toxin production.
    • MRSA coverage (vancomycin, linezolid, daptomycin) if suspected.
Organ/space infections
  • Intra-abdominal abscess and infection
  • Advanced CT imaging has enabled successful nonoperative management of certain intra-abdominal infections, including:
    • Acute diverticulitis.
    • Acute perforated appendicitis.
  • Percutaneous Drainage vs Surgery
    • Percutaneous drainage + antibiotics can treat peri- appendiceal, peri-colonic, and other contained abscesses effectively.
    • Surgical drainage is needed if:
    • Percutaneous drainage is not feasible (e.g., inaccessible location).
    • The infected organ needs removal (e.g., appendectomy, colectomy).
    • Small abscesses (<3-4 cm):
    • Can be treated with antibiotics alone in stable patients without peritoneal signs.
  • Duration of Antibiotic Therapy
    • 4 days of antibiotics after successful source control is sufficient.
    • Longer courses do not improve outcomes.
  • Practical Guidance
    • Stable patients without peritonitis:
    • Percutaneous drainage + 4 days of antibiotics.
    • Unstable patients OR non-drainable abscesses:
    • Surgical drainage + removal of infected organ.
  • Empyema
  • Empyema is a pus collection in the pleural cavity.
  • Most commonly occurs secondary to bacterial pneumonia and parapneumonic effusions.
  • Initial Management
    • Antibiotics + Tube Thoracostomy (Chest Tube Drainage)
    • First-line treatment: broad-spectrum antibiotics.
    • Tube thoracostomy (chest tube) is used to drain pus and expand the lung.
    • If chest tube drainage fails → Surgical intervention is required.
  • Surgical Management
    • Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS)
    • Minimally invasive.
    • Used to break up loculations and decorticate (remove fibrin deposits).
    • Open Thoracotomy
    • More invasive.
    • Used when VATS is insufficient for complete drainage.
    • Eloesser Flap or Window (for Recurrent/Persistent Empyema)
    • In cases of chronic empyema, a permanent drainage track is created between the pleural cavity and the skin.
  • Clostridium difficile colitis
  • Clostridium difficile (C. difficile) is a gram-positive, spore-forming anaerobic bacterium.
  • Antibiotic use disrupts gut flora, leading to C. difficile overgrowth and colitis.
  • CDI ranges from mild diarrhea to fulminant colitis with sepsis and organ failure.
  • Risk Factors
    • Antibiotic use (most important risk factor):
    • High-risk antibiotics: fluoroquinolones, clindamycin, cephalosporins, and penicillin.
    • Hospitalization & Healthcare Exposure:
    • Transmission occurs via contaminated hands and surfaces.
    • Other Risk Factors:
    • Advanced age (> 65 years).
    • Recent hospitalization or surgery.
    • Immunosuppression (e.g., chemotherapy, steroids, organ transplant).
    • Prolonged proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use.
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Watery diarrhea (≥3 loose stools in 24 hours).
    • Lower abdominal pain & cramping.
    • Fever, leukocytosis (>15K), malaise.
    • Severe Disease:
    • Fulminant colitis → hypotension, toxic megacolon, shock, and multi-organ dysfunction (MODS).
    • Peritoneal signs (guarding, rebound tenderness) suggest perforation.
    • WBC > 35K, lactate > 5 mmol/L, leukopenia < 4K → poor prognosis.
  • Diagnosis
    • C. difficile toxin detection:
    • PCR for toxin genes (A & B) – rapid and sensitive.
    • Enzyme immunoassay (EIA) detects toxin A/B or glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH).
    • Stool culture (gold standard but slow).
    • Imaging:
    • CT abdomen/pelvis → colonic wall thickening, toxic megacolon.
    • Abdominal X-ray → thumbprinting (suggests inflammation).
  • Treatment
    • Mild to Moderate CDI:
    • First-line:
    • Oral vancomycin (125 mg for 10–14 days).
    • Oral fidaxomicin (200 mg for 10 days).
    • Alternative if vancomycin unavailable:
    • Oral metronidazole (500 mg for 10 days).
    • Severe or Fulminant CDI:
    • Vancomycin 500 mg + IV metronidazole 500 mg.
    • Vancomycin enema (if ileus present).
    • Surgical consultation.
    • Surgical Indications:
    • Subtotal colectomy with end-ileostomy for toxic megacolon, perforation, or sepsis.
    • Emerging Therapies
    • Fecal Microbiota Transplant (FMT):
    • Highly effective for recurrent CDI.
    • Restores healthy gut microbiota.
    • Bezlotoxumab:
    • Monoclonal antibody against toxin B.
    • Used in recurrent CDI cases.
